reproduced.claim: the deliberately retained historical narrative reads as history, not as a live claim
reproduced.method: read every retained passage the builder named - the narrative in refusals.py, the corpus revision_note and note, the defeating-entry-unknown-key case - and asked of each whether a reader would take it as a description of the artifact as it stands
reproduced.finding: CONFIRMED, and the builder was right to keep them. The refusals.py narrative is explicitly past tense (This table used to extract an artifact standing) and closes on the present state. The corpus revision_note describes the drafts and why they failed. The defeating-entry-unknown-key case must carry asserted_standing and settled_by as fixture data, because that is what proves the refusal. None of these reads as a live claim, and deleting them would lose the reason the contract has this shape, which is the part of the record hardest to reconstruct later. The useful distinction I would offer is narrower than history versus no history: the one passage that goes wrong is the one that begins as history and ends as a live present-tense claim in the same sentence. That is closed_key_set, and that is where the remaining error is. A sentence that mixes the two lets a stale number ride on the back of a true story.

dissented.claim_defeated: the class of stale key-count claims is closed (handover: I grepped every standing and key-count claim across all five landing paths and found two more; five sites, not three)
dissented.finding: There is a sixth site, and it is a key-count claim in the same contract key the repair used as its template. contracts/status-claims.json closed_key_set reads, in full: An entry carries exactly field, value, subject, claim_kind, detail and reference. A witness added asserted_standing, settled_by, authority and a resurrected standing_source to live entries and every one passed, because type-checking named keys never rejects an unnamed one. The set is now closed and an eighth key is refused. The first sentence correctly enumerates six keys. The middle sentence is already size-agnostic and is the exact wording the repair copied into the two refusals.py sites. The last sentence is still pinned to the seven-key entry of the standing era: with six allowed keys, the key that gets refused is the SEVENTH. I measured it rather than counting - adding one key to a live six-key entry produces a seven-key entry and earns ENTRY_UNKNOWN_KEY. The corpus says so correctly: conformance/fixtures/status-claims/cases.json case defeating-entry-unknown-key states type-checking six named keys never rejects a seventh. So the contract and the fixture that proves this very refusal disagree about the same rule by one, and the contract is the wrong one. An exhaustive ordinal sweep across all ten landing paths returns exactly two key-count ordinals: cases.json line 64, correct, and contracts/status-claims.json line 452, wrong. There is no seventh site.
dissented.consequence: Small and self-correcting for an attentive reader, who can count the six keys listed in the same sentence. It is reported because it is precisely the class the repair set out to close, because the builder asked to be told if a sixth was sitting somewhere he had not grepped, and because two artifacts in one commit now state the same mechanism with different numbers. It carries no behavioural risk: the check refuses a seventh key whatever the prose says, and no code reads this field. The residue is also instructive about how the class survives - the repair generalised the middle clause of this sentence and carried that generalisation to two other files, without reading to the end of the sentence it was copying from.
dissented.what_would_have_defeated_this_finding: changing the tail of closed_key_set to say that any key outside the set is refused, which is true at any size and matches the wording the repair adopted everywhere else; or, if a number is wanted, seventh rather than eighth. One clause.

landing_assessment.my_view: One clause from landable. Everything I was asked to check reproduces, the repair is real and correctly shaped - generalising the sentence so it cannot go stale again is a better fix than correcting a number - and the retained history is the right call. The single thing standing in the way is that closed_key_set still ends an eighth key is refused when the seventh is refused, and the corpus in the same commit says seventh. That is one clause in one field, it needs no design decision, and it sits in the path the grant already covers. I would confirm on a reading of a commit that fixes it, and I would not ask for anything else.

standing_supported: Supports OPEN to BUILT for the ten paths and supports the narrower claim that W4-B1 is repaired. The repair is prose-only, proven by AST equality with docstrings stripped rather than inferred from the diff; all five named sites are now true; the two sites the builder found and I had not are real, and the wording chosen - named keys never rejects an unnamed one - is size-agnostic and cannot go stale when the key set changes, which is a better answer than correcting a count. Behaviour is unmoved under my full first-reading battery re-run against the new commit. verify passes on both sides with a delta of exactly the two registered checks. It does not support BUILT to WITNESSED on one finding, which is the finding the builder asked me to look for: the class is not quite closed. contracts/status-claims.json closed_key_set still ends The set is now closed and an eighth key is refused. A live entry carries six keys, the seventh is what earns ENTRY_UNKNOWN_KEY, and the corpus case that proves this refusal says a seventh in the same commit. An exhaustive ordinal sweep across all ten paths finds exactly two key-count ordinals and this is the wrong one; there is no seventh site. The remaining error is one clause, carries no behavioural risk, and is in the same sentence whose middle clause the repair copied into two other files without reading to its end.

judgement_items.question: Unchanged from my first reading and still the only item I would put to Bdo: contracts/status-claims.json names decisions/0074 as its governing decision and that record cannot land with the code, because decisions/ is outside grant:standing-landing-loop. Should verify grade the decision and governed_by paths of a contract for existence, forcing a contract to land with its decision, or is a contract permitted to name its governing decision before the record exists?

Two rounds have now been spent on prose that described the artifact wrongly, and both were found by reading rather than by a check. The repair adopted a size-agnostic wording that cannot go stale, which is the durable fix for one sentence. Is it worth a check that greps a contract for keys no entry carries and no module reads, or is the honest answer that prose drift is caught by reading and this concern has now had enough of it?
